title: Embedding service backpressure, kernel pre-warm, and priority-aware admission to reduce tail latency
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem:
The embeddings endpoint shows a long p99 tail during mixed workloads: short single-item requests mingle with sporadic large-batched inference and model-variant fallbacks. Prior tickets focused on microbatch and kernel parameters, but production traces show a class of spikes caused by admission/backpressure failures and cold kernel states.

Goal:
Reduce p99 from ~420ms to <=220ms for the 1-8 item request profile under 95th percentile QPS for core customers, while keeping median within 10% of baseline and not exceeding current cost-per-embedding by more than 5%.

Hypothesis:
1) Small requests are getting delayed behind large in-flight batches because the queue drain and executor admit logic lacks per-request priority and head-of-line fairness.
2) Kernel invocation latency for less-frequently-used model quantizations is increased by cold-starts inside the serving process (JIT compilation, kernel selection, memory pages not warm). Pre-warming a small pool of kernels and introducing priority-aware admission will reduce the tail significantly.

Approach / Workplan:
- Instrumentation (M1): Add per-request priority tags, queue timestamps, and kernel-warmness counters to tracing and metrics. Create heatmap dashboard showing queue wait vs kernel-warmness by model variant. (owner: L. O'Connor)
- Admission controller (M2): Implement a lightweight priority-aware admission layer that:
  a) applies a latency budget per request class (interactive vs batch) and rejects/redirects requests that would exceed budget;
  b) maintains a small fast-path queue for short requests and guarantees periodic drain to prevent starvation.
- Kernel pre-warm pool (M3): On node startup and when a model variant becomes active, spawn N pre-warmed kernel contexts (configurable per SKU) that hold compiled kernels and a small KV cache primer. Provide a fallback path that uses the regular pool.
- Backpressure policy tuning (M4): Integrate with existing autoscaler signals so admission controller can throttle upstream on sustained high tail.
- Benchmarks & rollout (M5): Create CI perf harness simulating mixed workloads (1-2 item interactive, 8-32 item bulk) with 10% model-variant fallbacks. Run A/B on canary fleet 10% then 50% then full.

Success metrics:
- p99 for interactive profile reduced to <=220ms under target QPS
- p50 change within ±10%
- No more than 5% increase in average CPU/GPU utilization after pre-warm tuning
- Zero customer-facing error increase (client 4xx/5xx unchanged)

Risks & mitigations:
- Pre-warm memory overhead: limit pool size per-node and evict idle contexts after TTL. Add a config knob per dedicated SKU.
- Priority starvation of batch jobs: ensure admission controller guarantees minimal batch throughput by reserving a fraction of slots.
- Complexity in metrics: add end-to-end dashboard and synthetic slo tests to detect regression early.

Rollout plan:
1) Land instrumentation and metrics (M1) behind feature flag. Validate heatmaps.
2) Implement admission controller in a feature-flagged path; run canary at 1% traffic using canary autoscaling.
3) Add kernel pre-warm with conservative pool sizes; monitor memory and error rates.
4) Gradually increase canary traffic to 50% then 100% if safe.

Notes on measurement:
- Use existing per-request trace id and tokenized latency breakdowns. Add new tags: request_priority, admit_decision, kernel_warm_hit.
- Synthetic load generator located at: https://perf-redwood/embeds/harness (internal) will be extended to reproduce mixed patterns.

Documentation & follow-ups:
- Update runbooks for embedding-node memory pressure and kernel-eviction thresholds.
- Add a short RFC describing config knobs for dedicated customers who want zero pre-warm due to memory constraints.
